O Soma and Rudra, whatever disease has entered our *gaya*, our house, or the creatures belonging to the house, that disease, going everywhere in all directions, drive apart; that is, separate it from us. Further, *nirṛti*, misfortune, *parācaiḥ*, turned away; as it becomes *parāk*,

Drive her far away; ward her off. May auspicious things, *bhadrā*, be to us, *asme*, that is, to ours: *sauśravasāni*, foods and renown. *Sauśravasa* is the state of one who has good *śravas*; and *śravas* is food and renown.
- विषूचीं (*viṣūcīṃ*)—that disease, spreading everywhere, every one of them
- सौश्रवसानि (*sauśravasāni*)—possessed of food and the wealth of renown

O gods Soma and Rudra, whatever disease has entered our house, every one of those diseases spreading everywhere and contagious, destroy completely. Make the goddess of misfortune turn back and thrust her far away. May there be auspicious things for us, possessed of food and the wealth of renown.
Soma and Rudra, expel the wide-spread sickness that has entered into our dwellings; keep off Nirriti, so that she may be far away, and may prosperous means of sustenance be ours.

O Soma and Rudra, you two, in our bodies, that is, in our limbs, *asme*, for us, place, *dhattam*, hold, all these well-known remedies. Further, whatever sin, *enas*, exists, is found, that has been done by us and bound in our bodies, that sin *avasyatam*: destroy it, loosen it; the meaning is, make its binding slack. Release it also from us.
- विश्वा भेषजानि (*viśvā bheṣajāni*)—all the means of warding off disease
- कृतं (*kṛtaṃ*)—both what has been acquired by oneself
- बद्धं (*baddhaṃ*)—and what has stuck on through contact from outside
- यत् एनः आस्ति (*yat enaḥ āsti*)—whatever sin there is, all of that

O gods Soma and Rudra, you two together, fill our bodies with all the well-known means of warding off disease. Whatever sin there is in our limbs, both what has been acquired by oneself and what has stuck on through contact from outside, destroy all of it completely. Release it completely from us.
Soma and Rudra, grant all these medicaments (for the ailments of) our bodies : detach, set free, the perpetrated iniquity that has been bound up in our persons.

O Soma and Rudra, *tigmāyudhau*, having bright bows; *tigmahetī*, having sharp arrows; *suśevau*, bestowers of excellent happiness; *sumanasyamānā*, desiring good-minded praise, that is, being praised, being of good mind. You two here in this world, *naḥ*, us, *su*, exceedingly, *mṛḷatam*, make happy. From the noose of Varuṇa release us. Protect us, and guard us from dangers.

O gods Soma and Rudra, possessed of sharp weapons, possessed of pointed arrows, bestowers of excellent happiness, possessed of a favourable mind, make us exceedingly happy in this world. Release us from the bond of Varuṇa. Protect us well.
Sharp-weaponed, sharp-arrowed, profoundly-honoured Soma and Rudra, grant us happiness in this world : propitiated by our praise, preserve us : liberate us from the bonds of Varuna.

When, *samadām upasthe*, at the approach of battles, this king goes, *yāti*, in a coat of mail, *varmā*, clad in armour, then the form, *pratīka*, of the king girt with an iron coat of mail becomes like that of a cloud, *jīmūta*; as is the form of a cloud, so becomes his form; this is the meaning. O king, with a body *anāviddayā*, not wounded by enemies, conquer the enemies. May that famous majesty, *mahimā*, of the coat of mail protect you, *pipartu*; that is, may it guard you.
- समदां उपस्थे (*samadāṃ upasthe*)—in the neighbourhood of battles (at times of war)
- वर्मि (*varmi*)—the king who has put on an iron coat of mail
- अनाविद्धया (*anāviddhayā*)—not exposed to the blows of enemies
- वर्मणः (*varmaṇaḥ*)—of the iron coat of mail

When the king, clad in an iron coat of mail at times of war, moves about on the field of battle, his form is grave like a cloud. O king, win victory with a body that is not exposed to the blows of enemies. May the famous greatness of the iron coat of mail protect you.
When the mailed warrior advances in the front of battles, his form is like that of a cloud : with his body unwounded do you conquer ; may the strength of the armour defend you.

It appears that this sūkta was composed at a time when battle was close at hand, that is, on the day before the battle. In this sūkta there are prayers to, and descriptions of, the implements of war such as the bow, the bowstring and the chariot. It has been said in the introduction itself that this sūkta has its application for equipping the king for battle at the time of war and consecrating him with mantras. For many ṛks of this sūkta Yāska has given a derivation and explained the meaning. All that has been described in the special notes on the respective ṛks. In the Yajurveda also, that is, in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, this sūkta is recited with small differences (Tai. Saṃ. 4-6-6). There the ṛks 9 and 15 of this sūkta are not found. There is a difference in the order also. The derivation and explanation of the meaning of the word समद (*samada*) is given in the Special Topics of the second ṛk of this same sūkta.

With the bow, *dhanvanā*, by the bow, may we conquer the cattle, *gāḥ*, of the enemies; that is, may we bring them under our control. With the bow may we also conquer the battle. With the bow may we conquer the fierce, haughty, exceedingly intoxicated armies of the enemy. So Yāska: समदः समदो वात्तेः संमदो ना मदतेः (*samadaḥ samado vātteḥ saṃmado nā madateḥ*) (Ni. 9-17). May the bow do away with, *apakāma*, the desire of the enemy; may it bring about the loss of his desire. Further, with the bow may we conquer the enemies stationed in all directions, *pradiśaḥ*. The word *pradik* is used figuratively for the persons who stand there, as in the saying "the platforms cry out". The repetition of the word *dhanvan* and of the verb *jayate* is for the sake of emphasis.
- धन्वना (*dhanvanā*)—with the help of the bow
- आजिं (*ājiṃ*)—may we conquer the battle also
- जयेम (*jayema*)—may we conquer the armies of the enemy
- प्रदिशः (*pradiśaḥ*)—the enemies at the ends of the directions

May we conquer the cattle of the enemies with the help of the bow. With that same bow we shall conquer the battle. May we conquer with the bow the armies of the enemy, sharp with pride and frenzied. May our bow bring about the frustration of the enemy's hope. With the help of the bow may we conquer the enemies at the ends of the directions.
While giving the derivation of the word धनुः (*dhanuḥ*), Yāska has given this derivation for this ṛk—

धनुः । धनुर्धन्वतेर्गतिकर्मणः वधकर्मणो वा धन्वंत्यस्मादिषवः ॥ तस्यैषा भवति । धन्वना गा धन्वनाजिं जयेम धन्वना तीव्राः समदो जयेम । धनुः शत्रोरपकामं कृणोति धन्वनाः सर्वाः प्रदिशो जयेम ॥ इति सा निगदव्याख्याता । समदः समदो वात्तेः संमदो वा मदतेः ॥ (*dhanuḥ | dhanurdhanvatergatikarmaṇaḥ vadhakarmaṇo vā dhanvaṃtyasmādiṣavaḥ ‖ tasyaiṣā bhavati | dhanvanā gā dhanvanājiṃ jayema dhanvanā tīvrāḥ samado jayema | dhanuḥ śatrorapakāmaṃ kṛṇoti dhanvanāḥ sarvāḥ pradiśo jayema ‖ iti sā nigadavyākhyātā | samadaḥ samado vātteḥ saṃmado vā madateḥ ‖*) (Ni. 9-17)

The word धनुः (*dhanuḥ*) may be formed from the root *dhanvati*, which indicates the meaning of motion or going; or the root *dhanvati* has also the meaning "kill". Therefore the bow is so named because arrows are shot from the bow and go to the enemies; or, in the sense of killing, because the bow is a means of killing enemies, it is also named धनुस्सु (*dhanussu*). To explain the meaning of the word धनुः (*dhanuḥ*) they have taken this very ṛk beginning धन्वना (*dhanvanā*) as the example. Since the meaning is clear merely by reading this ṛk, no further explanation of it is necessary. That the word समद (*samada*) in this ṛk has the meaning of battle: the word समद (*samada*) is formed from the root अद् (*ad*), "eat", with the prefix सं (*saṃ*), and since in this battle there are such actions as eating one another, that is, laying waste, destroying, killing and so on, the meaning of battle has come into usage for the word समद (*samada*). Or it may be formed from the root *madati*, which has the meaning "fight in anger". Then also the prefix सं (*saṃ*) joins the word *mada* and it becomes संमद (*saṃmada*) or समद (*samada*), and the word समद (*samada*) has the meaning of a battle in which they fight one another in anger.
May we conquer the cattle (of the enemies) with the bow : with the bow may we be victorious in battle : may we overcome our fierce-exulting
(enemies) with the bow : may the bow disappoint the hope of the foe: may we subdue with the bow all (hostile) countries.

In the preceding two ṛks the coat of mail and the bow are praised; here the bowstring is praised. This bowstring, *samane*, in battle, on the bow, *dhanvan*, stretched, *vitatā*, and bringing across, *pārayantī*, that is, carrying to the farther shore, comes, *ā ganīganti*, to the ear, *karṇam*, the ear-region of the king who holds the bow, as if about to speak an agreeable word, *priyam*, a word that gives pleasure. A woman, *yoṣā*, embracing, like a wife her friend, her husband, utters a sound, *śiṅkte*. So Yāska: वक्ष्यंतीवागच्छति कर्णं प्रियमिव सखायमिषुं परिष्वजमाना योषेव शिंक्ते शब्दं करोति वितताधि धनुषि ज्येयं समने संग्रामे पारयंती पारं नयंती । (*vakṣyaṃtīvāgacchati karṇaṃ priyamiva sakhāyamiṣuṃ pariṣvajamānā yoṣeva śiṃkte śabdaṃ karoti vitatādhi dhanuṣi jyeyaṃ samane saṃgrāme pārayaṃtī pāraṃ nayaṃtī |*) (Ni. 9-18).
- इयं ज्या (*iyaṃ jyā*)—this string of the bow
- पारयंती (*pārayaṃtī*)—joining and tying firmly the two ends
- वक्ष्यंतीव (*vakṣyaṃtīva*)—as if it were about to say
- आ गनीगंति इत् (*ā ganīgaṃti it*)—it approaches
- शिंक्ते (*śiṃkte*)—it makes a sound near the king's ear

This string of the bow, growing stretched out in battle and joining the two ends of the bow and tying them firmly, approaches the ear-region of the king who holds the bow, as if it were saying an agreeable speech, and makes a sound. Like women who embrace their beloved husband and speak, it makes a sound near the king's ear.

This bowstring, drawn tight upon the bow, and making way in battle, repeatedly approaches the ear (of the warrior), as if embracing its friend (the arrow), and proposing to say something agreeable, as a woman whispers (to her husband).

In the previous two ṛks the coat of mail (Armour) and the bow (Bow) used in battle were praised. In this ṛk the string, or bowstring, of the bow is described. The bowstring is the cord or rope tied to the stave of the bow (Bow-string). Instead of this cord or rope a strip of leather (thin shrip of a hide) or a sinew is also sometimes used. It must be very strong. And the stave of the bow must also be of a yielding nature. From the most ancient times the bow and arrows have been the chief weapons used in battles and the like. Even now, in many countries, bows and arrows are the chief weapons of the uncivilised forest people who live in hills and forests. These people display great skill in using them. They even kill large animals such as the elephant with the bow. On many occasions the tips of arrows are dipped in a juice or poison prepared from certain kinds of herbs and used so. Among forest people this is still in practice. Such a poison-smeared arrow causes very cruel wounds and the like and kills the enemy very quickly. On many occasions there is not even an opportunity to apply a proper remedy for it. That this practice also was in use in the age of the Ṛgveda is seen from what is said in the fifteenth ṛk of this sūkta. The Āryan people had to fight with the forest people (Dasyu), the former inhabitants of this country, who were armed with such poisoned arrows.

इयं ज्या समने धन्वन् अधि वितता पारयंती (*iyaṃ jyā samane dhanvan adhi vitatā pārayaṃtī*)—This string tied to the bow, making the twang in battle, is spread far and wide everywhere by this sound. When an arrow is fitted on the string of the bow, drawn as far as the ear and let go aimed at the enemies, it makes a kind of twang. Since hundreds and thousands of bows in both armies make this sound in battle, this sound spreads everywhere and pervades the whole battlefield; this is the main purport.

प्रियं वक्ष्यंतीव इत् आ गनीगंति कर्ण० (*priyaṃ vakṣyaṃtīva it ā ganīgaṃti karṇa0*)—प्रियकरं वाक्यं वक्ष्यंतीव धन्विनो राज्ञः कर्णप्रदेशं आगच्छंति । (*priyakaraṃ vākyaṃ vakṣyaṃtīva dhanvino rājñaḥ karṇapradeśaṃ āgacchaṃti |*) When an arrow is fitted on the bow and let go at the enemies, it is the practice to draw that arrow as far as the ear and let go. The farther back it is drawn and let go, the more forcefully and swiftly the arrow goes near the enemy and kills him. The seer has described very well, by two kinds of similes, this fitting of the arrow and drawing it as far as the ear. The meaning of the first simile is that the arrow fitted on the bow goes near the ear-region of the king who holds the bow, as if to say, or in order to say, an agreeable word in his ear. In worldly practice, those who say a beneficial good word go close to the ear and say it so that only that one person hears, and others who may be at the side do not hear. In the same way, this string with the arrow appears as if it had gone to the ear-region of the king who holds the bow, to say an agreeable speech to him, and were making a sound; this is the main purport of this simile.

सखायं परिषस्वजाना योषेव शिंक्ते (*sakhāyaṃ pariṣasvajānā yoṣeva śiṃkte*)—Now another simile will be given. Like a young woman who embraces her beloved husband and says a secret word in his ear, this string of the bow goes near the king's ear and makes there an agreeable sound; this is the purport of this sentence. Or these two sentences may be taken as one sentence and the meaning also given. The sound produced when, in battle, the king or the warrior fits an arrow on the string of the bow, draws it as far as his ear and lets it go at the enemy, is as if his beloved companion, his wife, embracing him, went near his ear to say, secretly, so that others do not hear, secret and agreeable words; this purport also may be given.
Yāska, in order to give the derivation of the word ज्या (*jyā*), has taken this very ṛk as the example and given the derivation for this ṛk—

ज्या ! ज्या जयतेर्वा, जिनातेर्वा, प्रजावयतीपूनिति वा ! तस्यैषा भवति । वक्ष्यंतीवेदा गनीगंति कर्णं प्रियं सखायं परिषस्वजाना । योषेव शिंक्ते वितताधि धन्वन् ज्या इयं समने पारयंती ॥ वक्ष्यंतीवागच्छृति कर्णं प्रियमिव सखायमिषुं परिष्त्वजाना योषेव शिंक्ते शब्दं करोति वितताधि धनुषि ज्येयं समने संग्रामे पारयंती पारं नयंती ॥ (*jyā ! jyā jayatervā, jinātervā, prajāvayatīpūniti vā ! tasyaiṣā bhavati | vakṣyaṃtīvedā ganīgaṃti karṇaṃ priyaṃ sakhāyaṃ pariṣasvajānā | yoṣeva śiṃkte vitatādhi dhanvan jyā iyaṃ samane pārayaṃtī ‖ vakṣyaṃtīvāgacchṛti karṇaṃ priyamiva sakhāyamiṣuṃ pariṣtvajānā yoṣeva śiṃkte śabdaṃ karoti vitatādhi dhanuṣi jyeyaṃ samane saṃgrāme pārayaṃtī pāraṃ nayaṃtī ‖*) (Ni. 9-18)

The word ज्या (*jyā*) (bowstring) may be formed from the root जि (*ji*) (jay), or from the root जिनाति (*jināti*), which has the meaning "conquer". Or, because arrows go out of this string very quickly, it has the name ज्या (*jyā*). In this ṛk (the present ṛk beginning वक्ष्यंतीव (*vakṣyaṃtīva*)) its meaning and use are explained. When an arrow is fitted on this string, drawn as far as the ear and let go, this string approaches the ear-region of him who lets go, in order to speak an agreeable word. Or, like a young woman who embraces her beloved friend or beloved husband and says a secret word in his ear, it makes an indistinct sound. The voice of women is not rough like that of men, but soft and somewhat shrill. The sound of this string also, like that, is shrill like a woman's voice and soft and sweet. When the arrow is fitted and drawn, this string also is stretched out lengthwise (stretches). समने (*samane*) means battle or fight. The main purport of the derivation is: may the string of such a bow win us victory in battles and the like and bring us across out of dangers.

Here the two tips of the bow are praised. Those two tips of the bow, *samaneva*, as if of one mind, as a woman does not leave the side of her husband, so moving about, *ācarantī*, going about on both sides, in the lap, *upastha*, in the nearness, like a mother her son

As a mother holds her son, so may they bear, that is, hold up, the king. Further, these two tips of the bow, *saṃvidāne*, agreeing together, free from disagreement, going as *ārtnī*. May the two, harming, *viṣṇurantī*, the foes of this king, pierce away the enemies. So Yāska: ते आचरंत्यौ समनसाविव योषे मातेव पुत्रं बिभृतामुपस्थ उपस्थानेऽपविध्यतां शत्रून् संविदाने आर्त्न्याविमे विघ्नत्यावमित्रान् (*te ācaraṃtyau samanasāviva yoṣe māteva putraṃ bibhṛtāmupastha upasthāne 'pavidhyatāṃ śatrūn saṃvidāne ārtnyāvime vighnatyāvamitrān*) (Ni. 9-40).
- पुत्रं इव (*putraṃ iva*)—as she holds a son (on her thigh)
- ते (*te*)—these two tips of the bow (the front parts)
- इमे (*ime*)—these same tips of the bow
- संविदाने (*saṃvidāne*)—in one and the same manner
- अप विध्यतां (*apa vidhyatāṃ*)—may they drive far away

Like a wife of loving mind, ever staying close by, and as a mother holds on her lap the son who is on her thigh, may these front parts of the bow bear the king. May these same tips of the bow, moving in one and the same manner and harassing the adversaries, drive the enemies far away.

May the two extremities of the bow, acting consentaneously, like a wife sympathizing (with her husband), uphold (the warrior), as a mother nurses her child upon her lap ; and may they, moving concurrently, and harassing the foe, scatter his enemies.
In this ṛk the two tips of the bow, called आर्त्नी (*ārtnī*), are praised. In describing them the seer has given the simile of women as the example. For this ṛk also Yāska has given a derivation—

आर्त्नी । आर्त्नी आर्तन्यौ वारण्यौ वारिषण्यौ वा । तयोरेषा भवति॥ ते आचरंती समनेव योषा मातेव पुत्रं बिभृतामुपस्थे । अप शत्रून्विध्यतां संविदाने आर्त्नी इमे विष्णुरंती अमित्रान् ॥ ते आचरंत्यौ समनसाविव योषे मातेव पुत्रं बिभृतामुपस्थ उपस्थानेऽपविध्यतां शत्रून् संविदाने आर्त्या विमे विघ्नत्यावमित्रान् ॥ (*ārtnī | ārtnī ārtanyau vāraṇyau vāriṣaṇyau vā | tayoreṣā bhavati‖ te ācaraṃtī samaneva yoṣā māteva putraṃ bibhṛtāmupasthe | apa śatrūnvidhyatāṃ saṃvidāne ārtnī ime viṣṇuraṃtī amitrān ‖ te ācaraṃtyau samanasāviva yoṣe māteva putraṃ bibhṛtāmupastha upasthāne 'pavidhyatāṃ śatrūn saṃvidāne ārtyā vime vighnatyāvamitrān ‖*) (Ni. 9-40)

In this ṛk also there are two similes. First the derivation of the form of the word आर्त्नि (*ārtni*) will be given. आर्त्नि (*ārtni*) is a word in the dual number of the nominative case. The word आर्त्नि (*ārtni*) may be formed from the root ऋ-गतौ (*ṛ-gatau*), which has the meaning "go" (आर्तन्यौ (*ārtanyau*)), or because the tips are made of wood (wood or bamboo stave) (अरण्यौ (*araṇyau*)), or from the word अरिषण्यौ (*ariṣaṇyau*), which has the meaning "kill enemies". That is: since the tips (the ārtnis) of this bow send the arrows out of the bow, it may be formed from the root *ṛ*, which has the meaning "go". Or अरण्यौ (*araṇyau*) means that, since this bow is made from a special tree born in the forest, the tips of this bow are made of wood; so it may be formed from the word *araṇi*, which indicates that meaning. Or, according to the meaning suggested in the word वारिषण्यौ (*vāriṣaṇyau*), because the arrows that go out with the help of the tips of this bow kill the *ari*, that is, the enemies, the name आर्त्नि (*ārtni*) has come; this is the purport of the derivation.

To make clear the meaning and use of this word आर्ति (*ārti*), he has taken the present ṛk beginning ते आचरंती (*te ācaraṃtī*) itself as the example and given a derivation for it. In the bow there are two tips, called the upper and the lower. These two tips are like two women. When one husband has two wives and both of them tend the husband who is equally joined to both of them, just as the minds of both co-operate in one and the same manner towards their husband and they behave accordingly, so the two tips of the bow co-operate and work when the arrow is let go from the string. Both tips bend equally, to one and the same level. There is no possibility that one bends more and the other less. As if there were mutual co-operation, both tips bend at the same time to the same level and help the arrow to go out of the bow. This matter the seer has explained by the simile sentence आचरंती समनेव योषा (*ācaraṃtī samaneva yoṣā*). This is the first simile. The sentence मातेव पुत्रं बिभृतामुपस्थे (*māteva putraṃ bibhṛtāmupasthe*) and so on is the second simile. As a mother holds her infant upon her thighs, these tips of the bow, harassing the king's enemies in battle by their strength and capacity and helping to kill them, hold, that is, protect, the king, who is like her son. A mother protects her child from various troubles

and dangers. Likewise these tips of the bow, being like a mother to the king, harass in battle, by means of the arrows that go out with their help, the enemy people who cause him trouble, destroy them, and protect the king from distress; this is the main purport of the derivation and of the simile sentence.

The quiver is praised here. The quiver is the father of many arrows; because it is a cause of protection it is called a father. Since the word *iṣu* has both genders, the use *bahvīnām* occurs. The son of this quiver, the arrow, is many; for many arrows are placed in the quiver. Because it is the receptacle of arrows it is the *iṣudhi*. So Yāska: इषुधिरिषूणां निधानं (*iṣudhiriṣūṇāṃ nidhānaṃ*) (Ni. 9-13). चिश्चा कृणोति (*ciścā kṛṇoti*): चिश्च (*ciśca*) is an imitation of a sound; when the arrows are drawn out, the quiver makes the sound चिश्चा (*ciścā*). Further, the quiver, bound at the back of the king who holds the bow, having reached, *avagatya*, the battles, *samanā*, that is, having come to them, impelling the arrows, *prasūtaḥ*, संकाः (*saṃkāḥ*): those that together cry out, make a sound, are संकाः (*saṃkāḥ*), armies. It conquers all armies.
- पिता (*pitā*)—it is a place of shelter, like a father
- पुत्रः (*putraḥ*)—the arrow, in the form of a son
- चिश्चा (*ciścā*)—when arrows are drawn out, the sound "chiḥ chiḥ"
- पृष्ठे (*pṛṣṭhe*)—on the back of the bowman

This same quiver is a place of shelter, like a father, to many arrows. The arrow, in the form of a son of this quiver, is of a large number. When the arrows are drawn out it makes a sound. Bound at the back of the bowman, approaching the battles and impelling the arrows, it conquers all the armies that are making a sound.
The quiver, the parent of many, of whom many are the sons, clangs as it enters into the battle : slung at the back (of the warrior), prolific (of its shafts), it overcomes all shouting hosts.
In this ṛk the इषुधिः (*iṣudhiḥ*), that is, the quiver in which arrows are kept, is described. For this ṛk also Yāska has given a derivation—

इषुधिः । इषुधिरिषूणां निधानं । तस्यैषा भवति । बह्वीनां पिता बहुरस्य पुत्रश्चिश्चा कृणोति समनावगत्य । इषुधिः संकाः पृतनाश्च : सर्वाः पृष्ठे निनद्धो जयति प्रसूतः ॥ बहूनां पिता बहुरस्य पुत्र इतीषूनभिप्रेत्य प्रस्मयत इवापाप्रियमाणः शब्दानुकरणं वा । संकाः सचतेः संपूर्वाद्वा किरतेः । पृष्ठे निनद्धो जयति । प्रसूत इति व्याख्यातं ॥ (*iṣudhiḥ | iṣudhiriṣūṇāṃ nidhānaṃ | tasyaiṣā bhavati | bahvīnāṃ pitā bahurasya putraściścā kṛṇoti samanāvagatya | iṣudhiḥ saṃkāḥ pṛtanāśca : sarvāḥ pṛṣṭhe ninaddho jayati prasūtaḥ ‖ bahūnāṃ pitā bahurasya putra itīṣūnabhipretya prasmayata ivāpāpriyamāṇaḥ śabdānukaraṇaṃ vā | saṃkāḥ sacateḥ saṃpūrvādvā kirateḥ | pṛṣṭhe ninaddho jayati | prasūta iti vyākhyātaṃ ‖*) (Ni. 9-14)

इषु (*iṣu*) means an arrow. Therefore इषुधिरिषूणां निधानं (*iṣudhiriṣūṇāṃ nidhānaṃ*): the leather bag in which arrows are kept, or the quiver, is named इषुधिः (*iṣudhiḥ*). Since the word इषु (*iṣu*) is used in both the masculine and the feminine, in this ṛk the feminine word बह्नीनां (*bahnīnāṃ*) (of arrows) as an attribute and the masculine word पुत्रः (*putraḥ*) are used. बह्नीनां पिता (*bahnīnāṃ pitā*) means बहूनां पिता (*bahūnāṃ pitā*); here बह्वी (*bahvī*) means arrows that are numerous. In this iṣudhi, or quiver, there are many arrows. To them this iṣudhi is a पिता (*pitā*), that is, it is like a father or protector. Because it keeps the sharp edges (points) of the arrows from becoming blunt, it is said to be a protector. Therefore the sentence बह्नीनां पिता बहुरस्य पुत्रः (*bahnīnāṃ pitā bahurasya putraḥ*) has the meaning that this iṣudhi is the father or protector of many daughters (arrows), and that this iṣudhi has many sons (arrows). Here the word पुत्र (*putra*)

indicates the generic singular, so the plural meaning "many sons" must be given for this word. Since the word इषु (*iṣu*) is used in the feminine and in the masculine, here the feminine word is understood as daughters and the masculine word as sons. Although there is a difference of gender, there is no difference of meaning. The meaning is simply arrows. How? Even if a man has only many daughters or female children, they say of him that he is the father of many children; or even if a man has many sons or male children, they say of him too that he is the father of many children, or that he has many children. As they regard children, whether male or female, simply as children and say only "father of children", so here, whether the word इषु (*iṣu*) is used in the masculine or in the feminine, the meaning is only one, and therefore the bag in which they are kept is well known by the name इषुधिः (*iṣudhiḥ*). When arrows are drawn out of this quiver one by one, quickly, at the time of battle, a kind of sound "chiḥ chiḥ" arises. From this sound the impression arises that the quiver is laughing (giggling). This the seer has described by the sentence चिश्चा कृणोति (*ciścā kṛṇoti*). Or the meaning of the sentence चिश्चाकृणोति (*ciścākṛṇoti*) may be given as: the quiver is making the imitative sound "chiḥ chiḥ". चिश्चा (*ciścā*) means the imitative sound "chiḥ chiḥ". The word संकाः (*saṃkāḥ*) in this ṛk may be formed from the root *sacati*, which has the meaning "suffer distress", or from the root *kirati*, which has the meaning "scatter", with the prefix सं (*saṃ*). In battle it is natural to suffer distress from the blows of various weapons and to scatter and run in various directions in fear of the enemy's blows; so संकाः (*saṃkāḥ*) means the armies in which these things happen; or, as the commentator has explained, सह कायंति शब्दायंत इति संकाः पृतनाः (*saha kāyaṃti śabdāyaṃta iti saṃkāḥ pṛtanāḥ*), that is, because they gather together on the battlefield and make sounds such as war-cries and groaning in pain, संकाः (*saṃkāḥ*) may also be taken to mean armies. पृष्ठॆ निनद्दो जयति प्रसूतः (*pṛṣṭhè ninaddo jayati prasūtaḥ*)—when fighting, since it is necessary for the warriors, when they discharge arrows from the bow at the enemy, that arrows reach their hands quickly, it is the practice for them to tie this quiver containing the arrows behind them on the back, draw the arrows from it one by one, fit them to the string of the bow and discharge them at the enemy. Therefore it is said here that the quiver is tied on the back. The main purport is that such a quiver, urging the warrior on in battle and making him eager, brings victory to the warrior who uses it.

Here in the first half the charioteer is praised, and in the second half the reins, *abhīśu*. The good charioteer, *suṣārathiḥ*, standing in the chariot, drives, *nayati*, the horses, *vājinaḥ*, that are in front of him, wherever, *yatra yatra*, he wishes to lead them, there. The reins in the chariot, which are nooses extending over the necks of the horses and which are at the back, in the rear part of the chariot, restrain, *anu yacchanti*, the horses according to the mind of the charioteer. Of those reins, *abhīśūnām*, the greatness, *mahimānam*, praise, *panāyata*; O people, praise. So Yāska: रथे तिष्ठन्नयति वाजिनः पुरस्तात्सतो यत्र यत्र कामयते सुषारथिः कल्याणसारथिरभीशूनां महिमानं पूजयत मनः पश्चात्सतोऽनुयच्छंति रश्मयः । न (*rathe tiṣṭhannayati vājinaḥ purastātsato yatra yatra kāmayate suṣārathiḥ kalyāṇasārathirabhīśūnāṃ mahimānaṃ pūjayata manaḥ paścātsato 'nuyacchaṃti raśmayaḥ | na*) (Ni. 9-16) **GLOSS**.
- पुरः (*puraḥ*)—that are in front of him
- पश्चात् (*paścāt*)—the horses yoked to the rear part of the chariot
- मनः (*manaḥ*)—in accordance with the mind's resolve of the charioteer

The excellent charioteer, seated in the chariot, drives the horses that are in front of him to wherever he wishes to go. The nooses of those horses restrain the horses yoked to the rear part of the chariot in accordance with the mind's resolve of the charioteer. O praisers, praise the greatness of these reins (bridles).

The skilful charioteer, standing in the car, drives his horses before him wherever he will : praise the efficacy of the reins; for the reins from the back (of the car compel the steeds) to follow the intention of the driver).

In the first half of this Ṛk the charioteer is praised, and in the second half the bits or reins of the horses. Yāska, giving the explanation of this Ṛk, says—अभीशवो व्याख्याताः । तेषामेषा भवति । रथे तिष्ठन्नयति वाजिनः पुरो यत्र यत्र कामयते सुषारथिः । अभीशूनां महिमानं पनायत मनः पश्चादनु यच्छंति रश्मयः ॥ रथे तिष्ठन्नयति वाजिनः पुरस्तात् सतो यत्र यत्र कामयते । सुषारथिः कल्याणसारथिः । अभीशूनां महिमानं पूजयामि मनः पश्चात् संतोऽनुयच्छंति रश्मयः ॥ (*abhīśavo vyākhyātāḥ | teṣāmeṣā bhavati | rathe tiṣṭhannayati vājinaḥ puro yatra yatra kāmayate suṣārathiḥ | abhīśūnāṃ mahimānaṃ panāyata manaḥ paścādanu yacchaṃti raśmayaḥ ‖ rathe tiṣṭhannayati vājinaḥ purastāt sato yatra yatra kāmayate | suṣārathiḥ kalyāṇasārathiḥ | abhīśūnāṃ mahimānaṃ pūjayāmi manaḥ paścāt saṃto 'nuyacchaṃti raśmayaḥ ‖*) (Ni. 9-16). The charioteer who drives the chariot, seated in the chariot itself, takes the horses yoked in front of the chariot wherever he wishes to go, that is, he urges them to go. This charioteer is skilful and clever (skilful, well-trained) in controlling and driving the horses. In the chariot the charioteer sits at the back and the horses are in front of him. This being so, how is it possible to make those horses (urged by signs or by words) go where he wants? The charioteer does not use signs or words to urge the horses. Instead of them he uses bits or reins (reins). These reins are called abhīśu or raśmi (rope). These reins, with which the horses are bound, are in the hand of the charioteer. By the movements of these reins the charioteer, although he sits behind the horses, can make them go wherever he wants. The main purport of the explanation is: "I praise greatly this kind of greatness, that is, the power and capacity, of the reins."

Here the horses are praised. The horses, वृषपाणयः (*vṛṣapāṇayaḥ*), whose hoofs rain down dust, rush with the chariots, exerting speed, and make sharp, that is, very loud, sounds. Moreover, not fleeing, they trample with the tips of their feet the hostile enemies, the foes, and destroy them.
- वृष पाणयः (*vṛṣa pāṇayaḥ*)—raising dust with their hoofs
- रथेभिः सह (*rathebhiḥ saha*)—along with the chariots
- अनपव्ययंतः (*anapavyayaṃtaḥ*)—not running away, leaving their paths
- प्रपद्यैः (*prapadyaiḥ*)—with the fore-parts of their feet (hoofs)

The horses, raising dust with their hoofs and running along with the chariots, make exceedingly great sounds. Without running away from their paths, they destroy the adversaries and the enemies, trampling them with the fore-parts of their feet.

The horses raising the dust with their hoofs, rushing on with the chariots, utter loud neighings, retreating not (from the charge), but trampling with their fore feet upon the enemies, they destroy them.

In this Ṛk there is praise of horses; that is, the action of horses on the battlefield is described. At the time of battle the horses of the chariots, urged on by the charioteers, run swiftly and charge upon the enemy armies. When they charge forward thus, the dust on the earth rises up through the swiftness of their going; that is, the dust of the earth rises from the hoofs of many horses. And

the horses, with great zeal, neigh loudly as though they themselves had taken an interest in the battle. Even while moving swiftly they do not go wherever they please, but charge upon the enemy army only in accordance with the charioteer's wish. The enemy soldiers, caught under their trampling, meet destruction; that is, many enemy soldiers, caught under the treading of the horses' feet, die. Such praise of horses is described in this Ṛk.

The wealth of this king that is carried on the chariot after conquering the enemies becomes an oblation; it becomes, like Agni's oblation, a promoter of increase. He explains that नाम (*nāma*) is a particle of assent. In the chariot in which this king's weapons, bow, arrows and the like, and armour are placed, to that chariot, bringing happiness, at all times, with happy minds, we, the Pāyus, the Bharadvājas, would approach it.
- रथवाहनं (*rathavāhanaṃ*)—the wealth brought in the chariot (after conquering the enemies)
- आयुधं (*āyudhaṃ*)—the weapons such as the bow

The wealth of this king, brought in the chariot after conquering the enemies, is fit for oblation. This is certain. In which chariot the weapons of this king, such as the bow, and the armour made of metal
are placed, that same happiness-bringing chariot we, the descendants of Bharadvāja, would worship on all days, with joyful minds.
The spoil borne off in his car, in which his weapons and armour are deposited, is the appropriate oblation of the warrior ; therefore let us, exulting, daily do honour to the joy-bestowing car.
In this Ṛk there is praise of the chariot. The description of the chariot of the king who has returned victorious after fighting and winning is given here.

रथवाहनं हविरस्य नाम (*rathavāhanaṃ havirasya nāma*)—रथेनोद्यमानं (*rathenodyamānaṃ*) wealth!⟨NOTE:229⟩ In the earlier age it was the custom to conquer the enemies in battle, load the wealth and other things they had onto one's chariots and the like, and return to one's city. In the same way, when the king, victorious in battle, comes with the enemies' wealth loaded in his chariot, the sage suggests the meaning that such wealth will be used for oblations and the like in the sacrifices they perform. The commentator has explained the word नाम (*nāma*) as "it is certain".

यत्र आयुधं निहितमस्य वर्म (*yatra āyudhaṃ nihitamasya varma*)—And in that chariot, besides the wealth and other things obtained from the enemies, there are placed the weapons such as the bow, taken for the sake of battle, and the armour, that is, the coat of mail worn or taken to protect the body from being struck by the enemies' weapons.

तत्र रथं उप शग्मं सदेम विश्वाहा वयं सुमनस्यमानाः (*tatra rathaṃ upa śagmaṃ sadema viśvāhā vayaṃ sumanasyamānāḥ*)—Such a chariot, which has done us the service of gaining victory for us in battle, we shall always approach with joyful minds; that is, we shall look upon it with a feeling of reverence.
notes: ರಥೇನೋದ್ಯಮಾನಂ in the commentary; the bhāṣya block has ರಥೇನೋಹ್ಯಮಾನಂ

en: Here the guards of the chariot are praised. The पितरो (*pitaro*) are the protectors of the chariot. They are स्वादुषंसदः (*svāduṣaṃsadaḥ*): they sit amid the sweet food of the enemies, or they cause the enemies' food to perish. They are वयोधा (*vayodhā*), givers of food; कृच्छ्रेश्रित (*kṛcchreśrita*), those who give refuge in distress; शक्तीवंतः (*śaktīvaṃtaḥ*), having the śakti, a particular weapon, that is, spear in hand; or else śakti is strength, and they possess it. They are गभीरा (*gabhīrā*), unassailable; चित्रसेना (*citrasenā*), having a beautiful army; इषुबला (*iṣubalā*), having arrows as their strength; अमृध्रा (*amṛdhrā*), incapable of being injured; सतोवीराः (*satovīrāḥ*), having attained valour. And so Yāska says that तिरः (*tiraḥ*) and सतः (*sataḥ*) are used of what has been attained: तिरः (*tiraḥ*) is "crossed over", and सतः (*sataḥ*) is "refined" (Ni. 3-20). They are उरवो (*uravo*), great, and व्रातसाहाः (*vrātasāhāḥ*), they overcome multitudes.
- स्वादुषंसदः (*svāduṣaṃsadaḥ*)—seizing the enemies' food and keeping it in their own possession
- वयोधाः (*vayodhāḥ*)—givers of food to all of us
- कृच्छ्रेश्रितः (*kṛcchreśritaḥ*)—givers of refuge in time of calamity
- इषुबलाः (*iṣubalāḥ*)—having strength in the form of arrows
- सतोवीराः (*satovīrāḥ*)—possessed of the wealth of valour
- व्रातसाहाः (*vrātasāhāḥ*)—defeaters of the entire host of enemies

The guardians of this chariot are those who seize the enemies' food and keep it in their possession, givers of food to all of us, givers of refuge in time of calamity, bearers of powerful weapons, firm of mind, having an attractive army, having strength in the form of arrows, unhurt, possessed of the wealth of valour, having broad bodies, and defeaters of the entire host of enemies.
The guards (of chariot), revelling in the savoury (spoil), distributors of food, protectors in calamity, armed with spears, resolute, beautifully
arranged, strong in arrows, invincible, of heroic valour, robust, and conquerors of numerous hosts.
In this Ṛk there is a description of the ratha-gopas, that is, those who look after a chariot properly and protect it so that no harm may touch it (Guards).

In the earlier age, when two armies fought, it was the custom for the leaders in each army, and on many occasions even the kings of the respective countries, to fight seated in chariots. Ordinary warriors did not fight seated in chariots. Only famous men, the atirathas, mahārathas, army commanders, kings, great kings and emperors, fought seated in chariots. Therefore, for protecting the kings or the chariots in which they sat, only excellent warriors, equipped with weapons, skilled in the work of war and valiant, were appointed to this duty. Hence these chariot-guards were the bodyguards of kings (Body-Guards). To protect the king from danger to life in battle was their chief duty. For the life or death of the kings who took part in battle was the chief cause of victory or defeat in the battle. Therefore one can easily imagine how important the discharge of the duties of these chariot-guards was. These chariot-protectors too, fighting the enemies on the battlefield, seize the food and the like that the enemies have and bring it under their control. Therefore they provide the enemies' food (provisions) to their own side. Even while a terrible battle is going on, they are not in the least afraid, but with a grave bearing and a resolute mind they display their strength and capacity. Besides special army support to help them, they also have the aid of the weapons they carry, such as bow and arrow. Enemy warriors cannot harm these warriors equipped with such weapons. The main purport of this Ṛk is that they are men of great strength and valour.
सतोवीराः-प्राप्तवीर्याः (*satovīrāḥ-prāptavīryāḥ*)—those who have obtained valour, or strength and capacity.

To support the meaning "obtained" (prāpta) for the word सतः (*sataḥ*), the commentator has given Yāska's explanation: तिरः सत इति प्राप्तस्य । तिरस्तीर्णं भवति । सतः संस्कृतं भवति । तिरश्चिदर्यया परिवर्तियोत्तमदाभ्या । पात्रेव भिंदन् सत एति रक्षसः । इत्यपि निगमौ भवतः॥ (*tiraḥ sata iti prāptasya | tirastīrṇaṃ bhavati | sataḥ saṃskṛtaṃ bhavati | tiraścidaryayā parivartiyottamadābhyā | pātreva bhiṃdan sata eti rakṣasaḥ | ityapi nigamau bhavataḥ‖*) (Ni. 3-20). The two words तिरः सतः (*tiraḥ sataḥ*) are synonyms indicating one and the same meaning. For this the meaning is "prāpta", that is, obtained, attained. For the word तिरः (*tiraḥ*) the meaning of तीर्णं (*tīrṇaṃ*) is "crossed over";

that is, going from one place to another means crossing even the distance that lies between two regions; for the word सतः (*sataḥ*) the meaning of संस्कृतं (*saṃskṛtaṃ*) is "joined together, being one". These two words are both derived from the root सृ (*sṛ*), which means "to go", with the sense of joining together and going. In the present Ṛk the word सतः (*sataḥ*) indicates the meaning that valour (prowess) has joined itself to these men. The two sentences तिरश्चिदर्यमा (*tiraścidaryamā*)⟨NOTE:230⟩ and पात्रेव भिंदन् (*pātreva bhiṃdan*), given as examples in the explanation, are Vedic sentences. The chief purport of the explanation is that these sentences support for those words the meaning stated above.
उरवः—महांतः (*uravaḥ—mahāṃtaḥ*). Those who are long-armed (reaching to the knees), tall and of stout, well-nourished bodies, men of great strength and valour, or those of excellent qualities.
व्रातसाहाः (*vrātasāhāḥ*)—those who defeat and put to flight the host of enemy people in battles, or those who boldly face many enemies even when they come charging in a crowd.
notes: ತಿರಶ್ಚಿದರ್ಯಮಾ printed; the quotation above has ತಿರಶ್ಚಿದರ್ಯಯಾ

en: ब्राह्मणासो (*brāhmaṇāso*) means: O Brāhmaṇas. The fathers are ऋतावृध (*ṛtāvṛdha*), increasers of ṛta, that is, of the sacrifice (?)⟨NOTE:231⟩ or of truth; सोम्यासः (*somyāsaḥ*) means worthy of Soma, or procurers of Soma. So Yāska says: सोम्याः सोमसंपादिनः (*somyāḥ somasaṃpādinaḥ*) (Ni. 11-18). "Protect us." The later word रक्ष (*rakṣa*), which is singular, although other words intervene, is here understood as plural.

Moreover, may the faultless Heaven and Earth be auspicious to us, makers of happiness. May Pūṣan, the nourishing deity, also protect us from evil, from wrongdoing. May no enemy who speaks evil of us have power over us.
notes: ಋಜ್ಞಸ್ಯ printed; ಯಜ್ಞಸ್ಯ?

en: - माकिः ईशत (*mākiḥ īśata*)—may they certainly not exercise lordship over us

O Brāhmaṇas, protectors, increasers of truth, and procurers of Soma, protect us. May Heaven and Earth, free from sin, be bringers of auspiciousness to us. May the enemies who wish us harm certainly not exercise lordship over us.

May the Brahmins, the progenitors, presenters of the Soma, the observers of truth, protect us : may the faultless heaven and earth be propitious to us : may Pushan preserve us from misfortune, let no calumniator prevail over us.

In this Ṛk the sage prays to the Brāhmaṇas engaged in the performance of sacrificial rites, to Heaven and Earth, and to the god Pūṣan, that they protect him on the battlefield from the fear of enemies and from danger.

पितरः (*pitaraḥ*)—Two kinds of meaning can be given to this word. पितरः (*pitaraḥ*)—पालकाः (*pālakāḥ*): those who protect us from the violence of enemies. Or our forefathers, elders, the sage Aṅgirases, and so on.

सोम्यासः (*somyāsaḥ*)—सोमसंपादिनः (*somasaṃpādinaḥ*) (Ni. 1-19)⟨NOTE:232⟩: those who, in sacrifices and the like, crush the soma creepers, squeeze out the juice and prepare it for the pressings and so on; or those who are engaged in the sacrificial rites in which the pressing of the soma is the chief thing; the foremost of the Brāhmaṇas.
notes: ನಿ. ೧-೧೯ here; the bhāṣya block has ನಿ. ೧೧-೧೮

en: In this Ṛk the arrows are praised. सुपर्णं (*suparṇaṃ*): this arrow bears a good wing (feather). मृगो (*mṛgo*), a part of a deer, its horn, is the tooth (point) of this arrow; for some arrows have tooth-points. Or else the tooth of this arrow is मृगः (*mṛgaḥ*), one that hunts out the enemies. Moreover it is bound firmly with गोभिः (*gobhiḥ*), products of the cow, sinews; or else गौः (*gauḥ*) is a name of the bowstring, and it is bound with that, with a change of number here. So a Vedic passage says: वृक्षे वृक्षे नियता मीमयद्गौः (*vṛkṣe vṛkṣe niyatā mīmayadgauḥ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-27-22)⟨NOTE:233⟩; its meaning is: on each bow the bowstring, fixed in place, makes a sound. And so Yāska says: वृक्षे वृक्षे (*vṛkṣe vṛkṣe*) means on each bow; the tree takes its name from cutting (felling), and it stands on the ground; क्षा (*kṣā*) is the earth, from the root meaning "to dwell"; नियता मीमयद्गौः (*niyatā mīmayadgauḥ*) means the bowstring makes a sound, मीमयतिः (*mīmayatiḥ*) being a word for sound (Ni. 2.-6). प्रसूता (*prasūtā*): urged forward, it falls. In the battle where men run together and run apart, there may the arrows give us happiness. And so Yāska says, in the same sense, that the arrow bears a good wing, its tooth is of deer-horn, it falls bound with sinews when sent forth, and that where men run together and run apart there the arrows give shelter (Ni. 9-19).
notes: abbreviation ಋಗ್ವೇ. printed

en: - मृगः (*mṛgaḥ*)—is the horn of a deer
- सं च (*saṃ ca*)—both gathered in a crowd

This arrow bears an excellent wing (feathers). The horn of a deer is its fore-part. Joined with bowstrings and urged forth, it falls upon the enemies. In whatever battle the warriors run about, both gathered in a crowd and separately, there may these arrows bring us happiness.

The arrow puts on a (feathery) wing : the (horn of the) deer is its point: it is bound with the sinews of the cow : it alights where directed : whenever men assemble or disperse, there may the shafts fall for an advantage.
In this Ṛk, in the Ṛk that follows it, and in the 15th and 16th Ṛks, there is praise of the iṣu, that is, the arrow. In this Ṛk the explanation of some words is necessary.

सुपर्णं (*suparṇaṃ*)—an excellent feather or wing. The arrow that is fitted to the bow and shot at the enemy has the feathers of birds tied to it so that it may travel swiftly. Therefore, here, सुपर्णं वस्ते (*suparṇaṃ vaste*) describes that this arrow wears an excellent wing or feathers.

मृगो अस्या दंतः (*mṛgo asyā daṃtaḥ*)—Here Sāyaṇa has explained the word दंत (*daṃta*) as शृंग (*śṛṃga*), that is, horn. मृगो दंतः (*mṛgo daṃtaḥ*) means the horn of a deer. It is described here that the sharp horn of a deer is used as the shaft (stick) of the arrow. Or, at the tip of some arrows they fix the pointed teeth (of certain animals) and so make the arrow sharp. Therefore it may also be said to be an arrow made sharp with the teeth of an animal. Or, if we give the word मृग (*mṛga*) the meaning मृगयमाणः (*mṛgayamāṇaḥ*), then this arrow, shot from the bow in battle, goes seeking out the enemies; that is, the purport is that it strikes the bodies of the enemies aimed at and sticks in them.

गोभिः संनद्दा पतति प्रसूता (*gobhiḥ saṃnaddā patati prasūtā*)—गोभिः गोविकारैः स्नायुभिः संनद्दा सम्यक्बद्धा अथवा गौरिति ज्यानाम तया बद्धा । (*gobhiḥ govikāraiḥ snāyubhiḥ saṃnaddā samyakbaddhā athavā gauriti jyānāma tayā baddhā |*). Here the word गो (*go*) means made from the cow, that is, tightly bound with the thread-like sinews in the body of the cow; the meaning is that the feathers of birds are bound tightly to this arrow with the sinews (nerves) of the cow. Or, since the word गो (*go*) also means ज्या (*jyā*), the bowstring, it may also be understood as an arrow shot from the string (the rope of the bow). The purport is that such an arrow, urged by the warriors who fight, falls upon the enemies.
For this Ṛk⟨NOTE:234⟩ Yāska has given an explanation—

सुपर्णं वस्त्र इति वाजानभिप्रेत्य मृगमयोऽस्या दंतो मृगयतीर्वा गोभिः संनद्धा पतति प्रसूतेति व्याख्यातं यत्र नराः संद्रवंति च विद्रवंति च तत्रास्मभ्यमिषवः शर्म यच्छंतु शरणं संग्रामेषु ॥ (*suparṇaṃ vastra iti vājānabhipretya mṛgamayo 'syā daṃto mṛgayatīrvā gobhiḥ saṃnaddhā patati prasūteti vyākhyātaṃ yatra narāḥ saṃdravaṃti ca vidravaṃti ca tatrāsmabhyamiṣavaḥ śarma yacchaṃtu śaraṇaṃ saṃgrāmeṣu ‖*) (Ni. 9-19).

In order to indicate the wings that are tied to the arrow so that, going forth from the bow, it may travel swiftly to the enemy, the word सुपर्णं (*suparṇaṃ*) is used here. The point of that arrow is made of the horn of a deer. Or the use of the word मृग (*mṛga*) here indicates the meaning that the arrow goes seeking out the enemies. The wings of this arrow are tied tightly with the sinews of the cow. Such an arrow, urged by the warrior, falls upon the enemy. While the battle is going on, the warriors of both armies rush from this side to that and from that side to this. The chief purport of the explanation is: may our arrows give us protection in battles against the onslaught of these enemy warriors.
notes: ಈ ಮಕ್ಕಳಿಗೆ printed; ಈ ಋಕ್ಕಿಗೆ?

en: ऋजेते (*ṛjete*): the arrow, which goes straight. O arrow, increase us all round⟨NOTE:235⟩. May our bodies be like stone, unbreakable⟨NOTE:236⟩. Moreover, may Soma speak in our favour, speak with partiality. May Aditi also grant us happiness.
notes: ವೃಷ್ಠ in the bhāṣya, ವೃಜ್ಞ in the Saṃhitā-pāṭha
damaged words ಆತ್ಮಮವದಭೇದ್ಯಾ ವೃಥಾ

en: - परि वृंगि (*pari vṛṃgi*)—increase on all sides
- अश्मा भवतु (*aśmā bhavatu*)—may they be strong like a stone
- अधि ब्रवीतु (*adhi bravītu*)—may he speak words of affection
O arrow, increase us on all sides. May our bodies be strong like a stone. May the god Soma speak words of affection to us. May Aditi also give us happiness.
Straight-flying (arrow), defend us: may our bodies be stone : may Soma speak to us encouragement : may Aditi grant us success.

In this Ṛk also the arrow (iṣu) is praised: that the enemy arrows may not strike us in battle and hurt us, our bodies should be firm as stone, and the god Soma and the goddess Aditi should protect us by bringing us happiness.

अश्वाजनि (*aśvājani*) is the whip, the driver of the horses, with which, through you, the wise charioteers, riders of the horses, strike the सानु (*sānu*), that is, the सक्तीनि (*saktīni*), of these horses and also strike their hind parts. Such as you are, urge the horses in the battles. So Yāska says: they strike the सानून्येषां (*sānūnyeṣāṃ*), the सक्तीनि (*saktīni*) of these, सक्ति (*sakti*) being that to which the body is attached; and they strike the hind parts, जघनं (*jaghanaṃ*) being from the root जंघन्यतेः (*jaṃghanyateḥ*). अश्वाजनि प्रचेतसः (*aśvājani pracetasaḥ*): those of enlarged understanding urge the horses in the समत्सु (*samatsu*), the combats, the battles (Ni. 9-20).
- अश्वाजनि (*aśvājani*)—O whip (lash) that controls the horses
- (such as you are) समत्सु (*samatsu*)—in the battles
O whip, controller of the horses, charioteers of skilful understanding strike the back parts and the hind quarters of these horses by you alone. Such as you are, urge the horses in the battles.
Whip, with which the skilful (charioteers) lash their thighs and scourge their flanks, urge the horses in battles.

In this Ṛk the kaśā or whip, which is used to urge the horses, is praised. This whip is also named अश्वाजनि (*aśvājani*). In order to explain this word Yāska has given an explanation of this word and of this Ṛk.

अश्वाजनी । अश्वाजनीं कशेत्याहुः । कशा प्रकाशयति भयमश्वाय । कृष्यतेर्वाणूभावात् । वाक्‌पुनः प्रकाशयत्यर्थान् । खशया । क्रोशतीर्वा । अश्वकशाया एषा भवति ॥ आ जंघंति सान्वेषां जघना उप जिघ्नते । अश्वाजनि प्रचेतसोऽश्वान्त्समत्तु चोदय ॥ अघ्नंति सानून्येषां सरणानि सक्कीनि । सक्षिः सचतेरासक्तोऽस्मिन् कायः । जघनानि चोपघ्नंति । (*aśvājanī | aśvājanīṃ kaśetyāhuḥ | kaśā prakāśayati bhayamaśvāya | kṛṣyatervāṇūbhāvāt | vākpunaḥ prakāśayatyarthān | khaśayā | krośatīrvā | aśvakaśāyā eṣā bhavati ‖ ā jaṃghaṃti sānveṣāṃ jaghanā upa jighnate | aśvājani pracetaso 'śvāntsamattu codaya ‖ aghnaṃti sānūnyeṣāṃ saraṇāni sakkīni | sakṣiḥ sacaterāsakto 'smin kāyaḥ | jaghanāni copaghnaṃti |*)

जघनं जंघन्यते । अश्वाजनि प्रचेतसः प्रवृद्धचेतसोऽश्वान् समत्सु समरणेषु संग्रामेषु चोदय ॥ (*jaghanaṃ jaṃghanyate | aśvājani pracetasaḥ pravṛddhacetaso 'śvān samatsu samaraṇeṣu saṃgrāmeṣu codaya ‖*) (Ni. 9-19, 22)⟨NOTE:237⟩

आश्वाजनी (*āśvājanī*) means the whip used for striking the horse. It is also named कशा (*kaśā*). This कशा (*kaśā*), or whip, causes fear to the horse; that is, the horse is afraid of the stroke of the whip. The word कशा (*kaśā*) is derived from the root कृष्यति (*kṛṣyati*), which means "to pull". It is very slender. And the word कशा (*kaśā*) also has the meaning "speech"; for speech makes meanings manifest, therefore कशा (*kaśā*) means speech. Or, when one strikes a horse one lifts the whip up and strikes, so it (the whip) is above, or in the sky. Therefore, the meaning that it is शा (*śā*), abiding, in the ख (*kha*), the sky, being suggested, it is named खशा (*khaśā*) or कशा (*kaśā*). Or the word कशा (*kaśā*) may be derived from the root क्रोशति (*krośati*), which means "to cry out, to shout". By the stroke of this whip the horse cries out, that is, makes a sound. Therefore this whip has come to be called कशा (*kaśā*): such is the derivation of the form of the word कशा (*kaśā*) and the explanation of its meaning. To support this, Yāska has taken the present Ṛk beginning आ जंघंति (*ā jaṃghaṃti*) itself as the example and given the explanation.

With this whip they strike the horses' जघन (*jaghana*) region, that is, the region at the side of the thighs. These regions of the thighs are named सक्तीनि (*saktīni*). The word सक्ति (*sakti*) is derived from the root सक् (*sak*), which means "join, unite"; that is, the body is as if attached to or joined with the two thighs. Therefore these are named सक्तीनि (*saktīni*). सक्तीनि (*saktīni*) means the loins, the base of the thighs and the region of the rear. These regions, which are as if joined to the back, they strike with the whip. The word जघन (*jaghana*) is derived from the root जंघन्यतॆ (*jaṃghanyatè*), which means "to strike many times". The sage, praying to the whip, thus praises it: O whip, urge in battles these horses, which are possessed of intelligence and strength and are swift; such is the purport of the latter half of the present Ṛk.
notes: ನಿ. ೯-೧೯, ೨೨ printed; the bhāṣya block has ನಿ. ೯-೨೦

en: Here is the praise of the हस्तघ्न (*hastaghna*) that is to be bound on the forearm of the archer. It is called हस्तघ्न (*hastaghna*) because, standing on the forearm near the hand, it is struck by the bowstring. ज्याया हेतिं (*jyāyā hetiṃ*): warding off the harm that comes from the bowstring, with its body, the number being altered. अहिरिव (*ahiriva*): like a snake it winds round the बाहुं (*bāhuṃ*), the forearm (the word "arm" being used here in a secondary sense). पर्येति (*paryeti*): it winds round. Moreover, विश्वा वयुनानि (*viśvā vayunāni*) are all the things to be known, माया वयुनमिति (*māyā vayunamiti*) being read among the names of knowledge. विद्वान् (*vidvān*): knowing; पुमान् (*pumān*): the man, endowed with manhood, may himself protect the archer on all sides. So Yāska says: like a serpent it winds round the arm with its coils, protecting it from the stroke of the bowstring; the हस्तघ्न (*hastaghna*), knowing all kinds of knowledge; पुमान् (*pumān*) is one of many minds, or from पुंसतीर्वा (*puṃsatīrvā*) (Ni. 9-15).
- हस्तघ्नः (*hastaghnaḥ*)—the bracelet tied at the wrist (on the forearm)
- पर्येति (*paryeti*)—has wound round and clings to it
- परि पातु (*pari pātu*)—may he protect completely

The bracelet tied on the forearm, warding off the blow of the bowstring, has wound round the forearm with its body as a serpent coils round it. May the man who knows all kinds of knowledge protect the archer completely everywhere.

The ward of the fore-arm protecting it from the abrasion of the bow⁻ string, surrounds the arm like a snake with its convolutions: may the brave man, experienced in the arts of war, defend a combatant ou every side.

In this Ṛk a particular article called हस्तघ्न (*hastaghna*), which is tied on the hand (the hand part), is praised. In order to explain the meaning of this word Yāska has given an explanation of this Ṛk.

हस्तघ्नः । हस्तघ्नो हस्ते हन्यते । तस्यैषा भवति ॥ अहिरिव भोगैः पर्योति बाहुं ज्याया हेति परिबाधमानः । हस्तघ्नो विश्वा वयुनानि विद्वान्पुमान्सुमांसं परिपातु विश्वतः ॥ अहिरिव भोगैः परिवेष्टयति बाहुं ज्याया वधात् परित्रायणमाणो हस्तघ्नः सर्वाणि प्रज्ञानानि प्रजानन् । पुमान् पुरुमना भवति । पुंसतीर्वा ॥ (*hastaghnaḥ | hastaghno haste hanyate | tasyaiṣā bhavati ‖ ahiriva bhogaiḥ paryoti bāhuṃ jyāyā heti paribādhamānaḥ | hastaghno viśvā vayunāni vidvānpumānsumāṃsaṃ paripātu viśvataḥ ‖ ahiriva bhogaiḥ pariveṣṭayati bāhuṃ jyāyā vadhāt paritrāyaṇamāṇo hastaghnaḥ sarvāṇi prajñānāni prajānan | pumān purumanā bhavati | puṃsatīrvā ‖*) (Ni. 9-15).

The हस्तघ्न (*hastaghna*) is a long strip of leather (belt). They wind it round the front part of the hand like a bracelet and tie it. When one quickly draws arrows one by one from the quiver, fits them to the bowstring and shoots them at the enemy, a part of the hand keeps touching the bowstring again and again. Since the hand quickly touches the bowstring, there is the possibility that the part of the hand that is touched may be wounded and harmed. To prevent that they wind that part of the hand with a long strip of leather. Since only the leather strip touches the bowstring, no harm is caused to the hand. Yāska has explained the word हस्तघ्न (*hastaghna*) to mean that which is tightly bound on the hand, and that, since this strip strikes the ज्या (*jyā*), the bowstring, again and again, the strip is named हस्तघ्न (*hastaghna*). He has taken as the example the present Ṛk अहिरिव भोगैः (*ahiriva bhogaiḥ*), in which this word is used, and given the explanation. This हस्तघ्न (*hastaghna*), that is, the leather strip (Hand-guard), has wound round the warrior's hand as a snake winds round an arm. It protects the hand so that the hand does not touch the bowstring. How? As a discerning man who knows everything averts the danger that may befall himself or others, so this हस्तघ्न (*hastaghna*) protects the hand of him who wears it from all dangers. In this Ṛk the words पुमान् पुमांसं (*pumān pumāṃsaṃ*) are used. पुमान् (*pumān*) means पुरुमनाः (*purumanāḥ*), one who has a manifold mind, one who has good understanding or strength and capacity; that is, one who is wiser and stronger than women: such is the etymological meaning of the word पुमान् (*pumān*). Or this word may be derived from the root पुंसति (*puṃsati*), which means "to crush, to tread down". The meaning is: very strong.

notes: Saṃhitā block prints ೫ ॥, Pada block ೧೫ ॥

en: The arrow that is smeared with आलाक्ता (*ālāktā*), that is, with poison, has a killing head (the word रुरु (*ruru*) is derived from the root meaning to kill), or has a horn for a head. And moreover, the arrow whose mouth, its point, is of iron. पर्जन्यरेतसे (*parjanyaretase*): she whose seed is Parjanya; to her, who is the product of Parjanya, since the shaft of the arrow is produced by Parjanya, to that great goddess, the arrow, this obeisance is made.
- पर्जन्यरेतसे (*parjanyaretase*)—which is the work of Parjanya
- इदं नमः (*idaṃ namaḥ*)—this offering of homage

To that arrow which is mixed with poison and destroys enemies, and moreover whose point is made of iron, which is the work of Parjanya, of great form and divine nature, this offering of homage is made.
This praise (be offered) to the large celestial arrow, the growth of Parjanya, whose point is anointed with venom, whose blade is iron.

In this Ṛk and in the next there is a general description and praise of the arrow. Dipping the tip of the arrow in poison and shooting it is a custom that has come down from very ancient times. In many countries forest-dwellers still follow this custom even now. Even if the tip of the arrow touches the body and does not cause a great wound, since the poison-soaked tip touches the blood,

the enemy dies at once. In many cases they have made the tip of the arrow from a sharp iron edge. Besides this, there was also a belief that if arrows were consecrated with mantras and the like, their power of killing increased. It can be said without doubt, from the descriptions in these two Ṛks, that all these methods were in practice at that time.

O arrow, ब्रह्मसंतिते (*brahmasaṃtite*), sharpened by a mantra, शरन्ये (*śaranye*), skilled in killing, you, once discharged and hurled, fly away; go forth from this place and go. Reach the enemies, the hostile, and attain them. Among these enemies do not leave anyone at all remaining.
- ब्रह्मसंतिते (*brahmasaṃtite*)—made sharp with the help of a mantra
O arrow, made sharp with the help of a mantra and destroyer of enemies, discharged by us, go far away, approach the enemy. Spare no one among the enemies, destroy all.
Arrow, whetted by charms, fly when discharged : go, light amongst the adversaries : spare not one of the enemy.

In the battle where arrows fall like कुमारा विशिखा इव (*kumārā viśikhā iva*), like shaven boys, there may Brahmaṇaspati grant us शर्म (*śarma*), happiness, always. May Aditi also grant happiness. The repetition is for the sake of respect.
- विशिखा इव (*viśikhā iva*)—without a tuft of hair

As shaven youths without a tuft of hair move about at will, so in whatever battle arrows, being discharged, fall in a continuous stream, in that battle may Brahmaṇaspati give us happiness on all days, that is, protection so that no danger befalls us. May Aditi also bring about happiness for us.
Where arrows alight like shaven-headed boys : may Brahmanaspati, may aditi, grant us happiness ; grant us happiness every day.

कुमारा विशिखा इव (*kumārā viśikhā iva*)—मुंडिताः कुमारा इव (*muṃḍitāḥ kumārā iva*). The commentator has explained these words as "boys with shaved heads". No special point is seen in their being compared to arrows. There is no connection between the one and the other. On this matter the scholar Wilson writes thus—

कुमारा विशिखा इव (*kumārā viśikhā iva*)-like boys without the lock of hair left at shaving; मुंडितः मुंडः (*muṃḍitaḥ muṃḍaḥ*) shorn-headed ; the point of comparison is not very obvious, but it may mean, that the arrows fall where they list as boys before they are left with the lock of hair, before the religious tonsure, play about wherever they like.

This simile does not fit well here. It cannot be said what likeness there is between the arrows falling everywhere on the battlefield like raindrops and shaven boys. The sage's intention cannot be like this. These words can be explained in another way. शिखा (*śikhā*) means the flame of fire; विशिखाः (*viśikhāḥ*) are flames or sparks of fire that shine specially or brightly. कुमाराः (*kumārāḥ*) means those who are not big like well-grown men, boys, those small in form. That is, the words कुमारा विशिखाः (*kumārā viśikhāḥ*) mean small sparks. As, when a smith strikes heated iron with a hammer, small sparks fly and fall all around, that is, in every direction, so on this battlefield the arrows shot by the warriors go and fall everywhere. One can explain the meaning in one way thus: may Indra protect us from the fear of such arrows. But this kind of meaning too is only a conjecture; it cannot be said with certainty that it is the sage's intention.

O king, your vital parts, the places in which, when struck, one dies at once, I cover with armour. May King Soma, after the covering of the vital parts, clothe you with nectar. Moreover, may Varuṇa also make for you a happiness still wider. May all the gods rejoice after you as you conquer.

O king, I cover your vital parts with an iron armour. Afterwards may Soma the king fill your body completely with nectar. May Varuṇa bring you very great happiness. May all the gods applaud you, the victorious.
I cover your vital parts with armour ; may the royal Soma invest you with amarosia : may Varuna amplify your ample felicity : may the gods rejoice (at beholding you) triumphant.

Whoever is our own kinsman but takes no delight in us, and whoever is cast aside, become remote and standing at a distance, and wishes to kill us — all the gods are to strike him down. The mantra (*brahma*) is for me an armour that wards off arrows.
- स्वः (*svaḥ*)—a kinsman belonging to us, whether (or)
- निष्पृः (*niṣpṛḥ*)—a distant one, not a kinsman, whether ⟨NOTE:239⟩
- ब्रह्म (*brahma*)—the mantra that praises the gods
notes: ನಿಷ್ಪೃಃ printed here; the Pada-pāṭha has ನಿಷ್ಪೃತಿಃ

en: Whoever of our own kinsmen, or whoever of those who stand at a distance, wishes to kill us, all of them may all the gods strike down. The mantra that praises the gods is for us an iron armour that wards off the arrows of enemies.
Whoever, weather an unfriendly relative or a stranger, desires to kill us, may all the gods destroy him : prayer is my best armour.
The seer, placing faith in the power and capacity that lie in mantras, has praised the gods, praying that the mantra that praises the gods may protect us like a coat of armour.
वेदार्थस्य प्रकाशेन तमो हार्दं निवारयन् । पुमर्थांश्च तुरो देयाद्विद्यातीर्थमहेश्वरः ॥ (*vedārthasya prakāśena tamo hārdaṃ nivārayan | pumarthāṃśca turo deyādvidyātīrthamaheśvaraḥ ‖*) **GLOSS**

इति श्रीमद्राजाधिराज परमेश्वर वैदिकमार्गप्रवर्तक श्री वीरबुक्कभूपालसाम्राज्यधुरंधरेण सायणाचार्येण विरचिते माधवीये वेदार्थप्रकाशे ऋक्संहिताभाष्ये षष्ठं मंडलं समाप्तं ॥ (*iti śrīmadrājādhirāja parameśvara vaidikamārgapravartaka śrī vīrabukkabhūpālasāmrājyadhuraṃdhareṇa sāyaṇācāryeṇa viracite mādhavīye vedārthaprakāśe ṛksaṃhitābhāṣye ṣaṣṭhaṃ maṃḍalaṃ samāptaṃ ‖*)
Here ends the sixth maṇḍala of the Ṛgveda-saṃhitā, accompanied by the venerable Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya and by a Kannada translation.
यदक्षरपदभ्रष्टं मात्राहीनं तु यद्भवेत् । तत्सर्वं क्षम्यतां देव वागीश्वर नमोऽस्तुते ॥ (*yadakṣarapadabhraṣṭaṃ mātrāhīnaṃ tu yadbhavet | tatsarvaṃ kṣamyatāṃ deva vāgīśvara namo 'stute ‖*) **GLOSS**
वागीशाद्याः सुमनसः सर्वार्थानामुपक्रमे । यं नत्वा कृतकृत्याः स्युस्तं नमामि गजाननं ॥ (*vāgīśādyāḥ sumanasaḥ sarvārthānāmupakrame | yaṃ natvā kṛtakṛtyāḥ syustaṃ namāmi gajānanaṃ ‖*) **GLOSS**
यस्य निश्वसितं वेदा यो वेदेभ्योऽखिलं जगत् । निर्ममे तमहं वंदे विद्यातीर्थमहेश्वरं ॥ (*yasya niśvasitaṃ vedā yo vedebhyo 'khilaṃ jagat | nirmame tamahaṃ vaṃde vidyātīrthamaheśvaraṃ ‖*) **GLOSS**
वेदः शिवः शिवो वेदो वेदाध्यायी सदाशिवः । तस्मात्सर्वप्रयत्नेन वेदमेव सदा जपेत् ॥ (*vedaḥ śivaḥ śivo vedo vedādhyāyī sadāśivaḥ | tasmātsarvaprayatnena vedameva sadā japet ‖*) **GLOSS**
(with the explanation of the Kannada translation of the meaning)
The first chapter in the fifth Aṣṭaka.

Vasiṣṭha is the seer who beheld the seventh maṇḍala of the Ṛgveda-saṃhitā. In this maṇḍala there are 104 sūktas in all. Unlike the other maṇḍalas, this maṇḍala does not have many seers; Vasiṣṭha alone is the seer, and this is the special feature of this maṇḍala. In the Purāṇas and other works too the seer Vasiṣṭha is renowned as one of the seven seers and as one of great radiance. Between this seer Vasiṣṭha and the seer Viśvāmitra, enmity arose for some reason, and the course of action they pursued and other matters are described at length in the Purāṇas and other works. The root cause of this matter is hinted at to some extent in the Ṛgveda, and that very thing is told at length in the Purāṇas and other works. Now, in this introduction, we shall give a brief account of the seer Vasiṣṭha.
**A Brief Account of the Seer Vasiṣṭha**

The great seer Vasiṣṭha is most highly praised in the Ṛg and the other Saṃhitās and in the Brāhmaṇas and other works. In the Ṛk-saṃhitā the seventh maṇḍala is wholly renowned as the Vasiṣṭha-maṇḍala. This great seer, having attained the direct realisation of the spiritual principle, has in his works described and praised in many ways the secrets of the universe and the special glories of the Lord. In the present account the divine life of this great seer is divided into three parts and set forth: (1) first, his divine descent, his birth and his personal greatness; (2) second, his relation to the king named Sudāsa and its consequences; (3) third, the mutual enmity that arose between him and Viśvāmitra and its result. Having made this division, we shall show how these matters are described in Vedic passages, and afterwards briefly state the points made in the Purāṇas and other works.
**The birth of Vasiṣṭha and his surpassing greatness**
In the Ṛk-saṃhitā, in many places, Vasiṣṭha is praised as one sprung from a divine portion and as one possessing personal greatness. The manner of his birth is told in this way.

विद्युतो ज्योतिः परि संजिहानं मित्रावरुणा यदपश्यतां त्वा । तत्ते जन्मोतैकं वसिष्ठागस्यो यत्त्वा विश आजभार ॥ (*vidyuto jyotiḥ pari saṃjihānaṃ mitrāvaruṇā yadapaśyatāṃ tvā | tatte janmotaikaṃ vasiṣṭhāgasyo yattvā viśa ājabhāra ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-33-10)

O Vasiṣṭha, when you spread your own radiance and made your power manifest, then Mitra and Varuṇa saw you. Immediately afterwards your birth took place on the earth. This is only one of your many kinds of manifestation.

उतासि मैत्रावरुणो वसिष्ठोर्वश्या ब्रह्मन् मनसोधि जातः । द्रप्सं स्कन्नं ब्रह्मणा दैव्येन विश्वे देवाः पुष्करे त्वाददंत ॥ (*utāsi maitrāvaruṇo vasiṣṭhorvaśyā brahman manasodhi jātaḥ | drapsaṃ skannaṃ brahmaṇā daivyena viśve devāḥ puṣkare tvādadaṃta ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-33-11)

O Vasiṣṭha, from the power of the seed of Mitra and Varuṇa, which fell at the sight of Urvaśī, you were born according to her wish. Immediately all the gods too placed you, one sprung from a divine portion and endowed with a mass of Vedic knowledge, in the Puṣkara.

स प्रकेत उभयस्य प्रविद्वान्त्सहस्रदान उत वा सदानः । यमेन ततं परिधिं वयिष्यन्नप्सरसः परि जज्ञे वसिष्ठः ॥ (*sa praketa ubhayasya pravidvāntsahasradāna uta vā sadānaḥ | yamena tataṃ paridhiṃ vayiṣyannapsarasaḥ pari jajñe vasiṣṭhaḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-33-12)

This Vasiṣṭha, fully knowing the principles of both heaven and earth, is a giver of gifts of many kinds, or else he is himself the very form of giving. Covered with the cloth of saṃsāra spread out far and wide by Yama, the controller of the whole world, he was born on the earth from the womb of Urvaśī.

सत्रे ह जाताविषिता नमोभिः कुंभे रेतः सिषिचतुः समानं । ततो ह मान उदियाय मध्यात्ततो जातमृषिमाहुर्वसिष्ठं ॥ (*satre ha jātāviṣitā namobhiḥ kuṃbhe retaḥ siṣicatuḥ samānaṃ | tato ha māna udiyāya madhyāttato jātamṛṣimāhurvasiṣṭhaṃ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-33-13)

When Mitra and Varuṇa, initiated for the sacrifice, poured their seed into the common jar of a pot that had been set up with praise, there arose in the middle, out of that vessel called Vasatīvarī, the birth of Agastya, and afterwards, out of the same vessel, the birth of Vasiṣṭha.

उक्तभृतं सामभृतं बिभर्ति ग्रावाणं बिभ्रत्प्र वदात्यग्रे । उपैनमाध्वं सुमनस्यमाना आ वो गच्छाति प्रत्यदो वसिष्ठः ॥ (*uktabhṛtaṃ sāmabhṛtaṃ bibharti grāvāṇaṃ bibhratpra vadātyagre | upainamādhvaṃ sumanasyamānā ā vo gacchāti pratyado vasiṣṭhaḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-33-14)

O sacrificers called Pratṛt, the venerable Vasiṣṭha comes to you. ⟨NOTE:240⟩ Honour such a Vasiṣṭha. In your sacrifice he takes the place of the Brahman priest and is the guide of the reciters of the śastra-mantras, of the Udgātṛs, and of those engaged in the pressing rite. Therefore honour him and treat him with respect: such are the words of praise. The authors of the Bṛhaddevatā have explained this very matter as follows.

प्राजापत्यो मरीचिर्हि मारीचः कश्यपो मुनिः । तस्य देव्योऽभवज्जाया दाक्षायण्यस्रयोदश ॥ अदितिर्दितिर्दनुः काला दनायुः सिंहिका मुनिः । (*prājāpatyo marīcirhi mārīcaḥ kaśyapo muniḥ | tasya devyo 'bhavajjāyā dākṣāyaṇyasrayodaśa ‖ aditirditirdanuḥ kālā danāyuḥ siṃhikā muniḥ |*) (Bṛ. De. 5. 143,144)

Prajāpati obtained a son named Marīci. The son of Marīci was the great seer Kaśyapa. This Kaśyapa married thirteen divine maidens, daughters of Dakṣa. Those maidens bore the names Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kālā, Danāyu, Siṃhakā and so on.

तत्रैका त्वदितिर्देवी द्वादशाजनयत्सुतान् । भगश्चैवार्यमांशश्च मित्रो वरुण एव च । धाता चैव विधाता च विवस्वांश्च महाद्युतिः ॥ (*tatraikā tvaditirdevī dvādaśājanayatsutān | bhagaścaivāryamāṃśaśca mitro varuṇa eva ca | dhātā caiva vidhātā ca vivasvāṃśca mahādyutiḥ ‖*) (Bṛ. De. 5. 146,447) ⟨NOTE:241⟩
Among these daughters, Aditi, the goddess-natured, bore twelve sons: Bhaga, Arama, Aṃśa, Mitra, Varuṇa, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Vivasvān of great splendour, and

त्वष्टा पूषा तथैवेंद्रो द्वादशो विष्णुरुच्यते । द्वन्ध्वं तस्यास्तु तज्ञज्ञे मित्रश्च वरुणश्च ह ॥ (*tvaṣṭā pūṣā tathaiveṃdro dvādaśo viṣṇurucyate | dvandhvaṃ tasyāstu tajñajñe mitraśca varuṇaśca ha ‖*) (Bṛ. De. 5-148)
Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, Indra and Viṣṇu — these are the twelve children. Viṣṇu is the twelfth. Thus from this Aditi were born the pair Mitra and Varuṇa (the twins).
तयोरादित्ययोस्सत्ते दृष्ट्वाप्सरसमुर्वशीं । रेतश्चस्कंद तत्कुंभे न्यपतद्वासतीवरे ॥ (*tayorādityayossatte dṛṣṭvāpsarasamurvaśīṃ | retaścaskaṃda tatkuṃbhe nyapatadvāsatīvare ‖*) (Bṛ. De. 5-149)

Of these twelve Ādityas, Mitra and Varuṇa both saw, at the time of the sacrifice of the sattra kind, the divine woman Urvaśī. As soon as they saw her, their seed fell. Then it fell together into the vessel called Vasatīvarī.
तेनैव तु मुहूर्तेन वीर्यवंतौ तपस्विनौ । अगस्त्यश्च वसिष्ठश्च तत्रर्षि संबभूवतुः ॥ (*tenaiva tu muhūrtena vīryavaṃtau tapasvinau | agastyaśca vasiṣṭhaśca tatrarṣi saṃbabhūvatuḥ ‖*) (Bṛ. De. 5-150)
As soon as that seed fell into that vessel, the seers Agastya and Vasiṣṭha, mighty and ascetic, were born from it. The manner of their birth is this:

बहुधा पतिते शुक्रे कलशेऽथ जले स्थले । स्थले वसिष्ठस्तु मुनिः संभूत ऋषिसत्तमः ॥ (*bahudhā patite śukre kalaśe 'tha jale sthale | sthale vasiṣṭhastu muniḥ saṃbhūta ṛṣisattamaḥ ‖*) (Bṛ. De. 5-151) ⟨NOTE:242⟩

That seed, fallen from Mitra and Varuṇa, was divided in many ways. It was spilt in the jar, in the water and on the earth. From the portion spilt on the earth, the great seer Vasiṣṭha, the best of all seers, was born on the earth (Agastya was born in the jar, and Matsya in the water).

कुंभ इत्यभिधानं तु परिमाणस्य लक्ष्यते । ततोऽप्सु गृह्यमाणासु वसिष्ठिः पुष्करे स्थितः ॥ (*kuṃbha ityabhidhānaṃ tu parimāṇasya lakṣyate | tato 'psu gṛhyamāṇāsu vasiṣṭhiḥ puṣkare sthitaḥ ‖*) (Bṛ. De. 5-15) ⟨NOTE:243⟩

Because the jar, the source of the birth of the seer Agastya, was a means of measure, it came to be called by that name. At the time when the water was being drawn up, the great seer Vasiṣṭha was seen standing on the lotus (*puṣkara*). This very fact is described in the Ṛk quoted above by the words विश्वे देवाः पुष्करे त्वाददंतॆ (*viśve devāḥ puṣkare tvādadaṃtè*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-33-11). Explaining this Ṛk, the author of the Nirukta
has said सर्वे देवाः पुष्करे त्वाधारयंत (*sarve devāḥ puṣkare tvādhārayaṃta*) (Ni. 5-14).
सर्वत्र पुष्करं तत्र विश्वे देवा आधारयन् । उत्थाय सलिलात्तस्मादथ तेपे महत्तपः ॥ (*sarvatra puṣkaraṃ tatra viśve devā ādhārayan | utthāya salilāttasmādatha tepe mahattapaḥ ‖*) (Bṛ. De. 5-155)
At that time all the gods, in all directions, lifted up and held this Vasiṣṭha; so Vasiṣṭha was raised up from the lotus. Then, rising from it, Vasiṣṭha performed very great austerity.

नामास्य गुणतो जज्ञे वसतेः श्रैष्ठ्यकर्मणः । अदृश्यमृषिभिर्हिंंद्रं सोऽपश्यत्तपसा पुरा ॥ (*nāmāsya guṇato jajñe vasateḥ śraiṣṭhyakarmaṇaḥ | adṛśyamṛṣibhirhiṃṃdraṃ so 'paśyattapasā purā ‖*) (Bṛ. De. 5-156)

From the root *vas*, which denotes a most excellent act, the word Vasiṣṭha was formed, and it is a name that denotes the excellent qualities and deeds of this great seer. It is well known that this great seer obtained the sight of Indra, whom no other seers had been able to see before. For this very reason,
सोमभागानथो तस्मै प्रोवाच हरिवाहनः । ऋषयो वा इंद्रमिति ब्राह्मणात्तद्धि दृश्यते ॥ (*somabhāgānatho tasmai provāca harivāhanaḥ | ṛṣayo vā iṃdramiti brāhmaṇāttaddhi dṛśyate ‖*) (Bṛ. De. 5-157)

Because of those great qualities, Indra, the lord of the horses named Hari, declared: “This Vasiṣṭha too should have a share in the Soma.” This very occasion is told in the Brāhmaṇas and other works with the words ऋषयो वा इंद्रं (*ṛṣayo vā iṃdraṃ*) and so on. This account will be explained further on.

वसिष्ठश्च वसिष्ठाश्च ब्राह्मणा ब्रह्मकर्मणि । सर्वकर्मसु यज्ञेषु दक्षिणीयतमास्तथा ॥ (*vasiṣṭhaśca vasiṣṭhāśca brāhmaṇā brahmakarmaṇi | sarvakarmasu yajñeṣu dakṣiṇīyatamāstathā ‖*) (Bṛ. De. 5-158) ⟨NOTE:244⟩

Therefore Vasiṣṭha, and all the seers born in the family of Vasiṣṭha, used to hold the position of the priest called Brahman in all rites. This position, worthy of the best sacrificial fee in all rites, belonged to no one else but them.

तस्माद्येऽद्यापि वासिष्ठाः सदस्याः स्युस्तु कर्हिचित् । अर्हयेद्दक्षिणाभिस्तान् भाल्लवेया श्रुतिस्त्वियं ॥ (*tasmādye 'dyāpi vāsiṣṭhāḥ sadasyāḥ syustu karhicit | arhayeddakṣiṇābhistān bhāllaveyā śrutistviyaṃ ‖*) (Bṛ. De. 5-159)

Because of such power, even in the present age, in all sacrificial assemblies only those born in the family of Vasiṣṭha are to be chosen for this excellent position: so the Bhāllavī Śruti passage declares.
Thus there is yet another episode that tells the greatness of Vasiṣṭha, and it praises this seer's skill in action. Its particulars are as follows.

वरुणस्य गृहान्रात्रौ वसिष्ठः स्वप्न आचरत् । प्राविवेशाथ तं तत्र श्वा नदन्नभ्यधावत । क्रंदंतं सारमेयं स धावंतं दष्टुमुद्यतं ॥ (*varuṇasya gṛhānrātrau vasiṣṭhaḥ svapna ācarat | prāviveśātha taṃ tatra śvā nadannabhyadhāvata | kraṃdaṃtaṃ sārameyaṃ sa dhāvaṃtaṃ daṣṭumudyataṃ ‖*) (Bṛ. De. 6-11, 12)
In the night, in a dream, Vasiṣṭha entered the house of Varuṇa. At that time a dog chased after him. As that dog, seeing him, came running barking, intending to bite, he, wishing to pacify it,

यदर्जुनेति च द्वाभ्यां सांत्वयित्वा व्यसुष्वपत् । स तं प्रस्वापयामास जनमन्यं च वारुणं ॥ (*yadarjuneti ca dvābhyāṃ sāṃtvayitvā vyasuṣvapat | sa taṃ prasvāpayāmāsa janamanyaṃ ca vāruṇaṃ ‖*) (Bṛ. De. 6-13)

recited the mantras beginning यदर्जुन (*yadarjuna*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-55-2), well known in the Ṛk-saṃhitā, and made the dog fall asleep. In the same way he enchanted Varuṇa's other servants too, so that they slept.

ततस्तु वरुणो राजा स्वैः पाशैः प्रत्यबध्यत । स बद्धः पितरं सूक्तैश्च तुर्भिरित उत्तरैः ॥ (*tatastu varuṇo rājā svaiḥ pāśaiḥ pratyabadhyata | sa baddhaḥ pitaraṃ sūktaiśca turbhirita uttaraiḥ ‖*) (Bṛ. De. 6-14)

Varuṇa, seeing that the dog and the servants had thus been enchanted, came himself in person and bound Vasiṣṭha. Then Vasiṣṭha praised and extolled the father (Varuṇa) who had bound him with four sūktas.
अभितुष्टाव धीरेति मुमोचैनं ततः पिता । ध्रुवासु त्वेति चोक्तायां पाशा अस्मात्पमोचिरे ॥ (*abhituṣṭāva dhīreti mumocainaṃ tataḥ pitā | dhruvāsu tveti coktāyāṃ pāśā asmātpamocire ‖*) (Bṛ. De. 6-15)

Then Vasiṣṭha recited four sūktas, together with the sūkta that begins with the mantra धीरा त्वस्य महिना (*dhīrā tvasya mahinā*), and praised Varuṇa. Pleased with that, Varuṇa released Vasiṣṭha from his bonds. As soon as the mantra ध्रुवासु त्वासु (*dhruvāsu tvāsu*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-88-7) was recited, the noose with which Varuṇa had bound him came undone: thus Vasiṣṭha's skill in action is praised.

Thus the occasions on which Vasiṣṭha became the object of the displeasure of his father Varuṇa, and again the object of that same Varuṇa's favour, are specified in many places in the Ṛk-saṃhitā itself.

उवाच मे वरुणो मेधिराय त्रिः सप्त नामाघ्न्या बिभर्ति । विद्वान् पदस्य गुह्या न वोचद्युगाय विप्र उपराय शिक्षन् ॥ (*uvāca me varuṇo medhirāya triḥ sapta nāmāghnyā bibharti | vidvān padasya guhyā na vocadyugāya vipra uparāya śikṣan ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-87-4)

In this mantra Vasiṣṭha has told the nature of the teaching of knowledge that he received from Varuṇa. “Varuṇa has borne for me, the wise one, the Aghnyā (cow) having twenty-one (21) kinds of names; that is, he has taught me. He, the all-knowing, has also taught me, who am endowed with yoga, the most excellent secret of the world of Brahmā”: thus Vasiṣṭha has praised his father.
By the mantras beginning आ यद्रुहाव वरुणश्च नावं (*ā yadruhāva varuṇaśca nāvaṃ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-88-3), the close relation of Varuṇa and Vasiṣṭha is described, as explained below.

“When I (Vasiṣṭha) and Varuṇa together board the boat, launch it into the midst of the sea and move about in the midst of the water, then we enjoy the pleasure of rocking in the midst of the water. Varuṇa, from a father's affection, seated Vasiṣṭha in his boat, gave him his protection, and helped so that most excellent deeds were accomplished by him. He made all the days of that same Vasiṣṭha, his worshipper, most happy.” (7-88-3, 4)

In these and many other places it is described how, by the favour of Varuṇa, Vasiṣṭha performed good deeds and enjoyed the happiness that was their fruit. All this will be told in the respective contexts. Besides this, in some situations it is also indicated that Vasiṣṭha became the object of Varuṇa's displeasure.
